ordered_diagnoses: Myocardial Infarction with Non-Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease

facts.raw_span: paroxysmal chest pain
The chest pain had occurred 5 times during the day, and each episode lasted 15 to 30 minutes
blood pressure and pulse rate were 106/52 mm Hg and 64 beats per minutes
normal breath and heart sounds with no murmurs
Hemogram, serum electrolyte levels, kidney and liver function tests, B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer levels were all within normal limits
Cardiac troponin I level was 25 ng/mL (normal, <0.023 ng/mL)
sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevation in leads III and aVR, Q wave in lead III, and ST-segment depression in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, and V2 to V6
sinus bradycardia (46 beats per minute), Q-wave amplitude deepening, ST-segment falling back to equipotential line, and T-wave inversion in lead III
total occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery (LMCA)

concepts.why: The patient's elevated cardiac troponin I level, ST-segment elevation on ECG, and total occlusion of the right coronary artery are indicative of an acute myocardial infarction.
The patient's recurrent chest pain, ST-segment elevation and depression on ECG, and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery are suggestive of unstable angina.
The patient's elevated cardiac troponin I level, ST-segment depression on ECG, and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery are indicative of a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
The patient's ECG changes, total occlusion of the right coronary artery, and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery are indicative of coronary artery disease.
The patient's recurrent chest pain, elevated cardiac troponin I level, and ECG changes are indicative of cardiac ischemia.
The patient's ECG changes, total occlusion of the right coronary artery, and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery are indicative of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
The patient's recurrent chest pain, ST-segment elevation on ECG, and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery are suggestive of Prinzmetal's angina.
